title: Root Cause Hunt - Console Debug & Request Logs Walkthrough (Sequoia Education)
next_steps: Share short runbook for request-inspector and trace handoff
Schedule 2-hour pilot benchmark with Liam and Evan (week of Jan 6)
Provide pricing for 3-month dedicated pilot + SLA add-on
action_items: Maya Chen: Email SOC2 and KMS notes (due 2025-12-19)
Evan Brooks: Prep pilot runbook and test payloads (due 2025-12-30)
Priya Nair: Share sample prompt sets and 95th perc latency SLO (due 2025-12-23)
summary: Redwood AE + SE did a Console-driven root-cause debugging walkthrough for Sequoia Education focused on request logs, trace correlation, playback and error analysis. Customer emphasized intermittent 5xx spikes and tail latency at peak. Action: send security docs, run pilot, share runbook + pricing.
topics: Trace correlation across retries and fallback models
Retention and PII handling in logs
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time, really appreciate it. I see Priya, Liam, Aisha — thanks for joining. I'll hand off to Evan for the console demo focused on troubleshooting and root cause hunt, and then we'll circle back on next steps.

[00:18] Evan Brooks: Cool, hi all. Quick agenda: I'll walk request-inspector, traces, playback, and then show an example 5xx investigation. We'll keep it hands-on; feel free to interrupt.

[00:34] Priya Nair: Sounds good. Quick context — we've been seeing intermittent 5xx bursts during grading batch windows; they last maybe 5–10 minutes and correlate with a higher token churn. We're on a mixed stack: primarily OpenAI today, some internal caching, and using AWS EKS. We're evaluating Redwood for both hosted + private.

[00:56] Aisha Bello: Also important: we have strict PII masking policies and a 30-day log retention requirement for audit.

[01:10] Liam Ortega: And we need to see exact request payloads in the logs for debugging, but we can't have raw PII kept beyond parity with our policy.

[01:22] Evan Brooks: Great, we'll cover retention and redaction settings in the console. Okay jumping into the console — this is a demo tenant so you might see synthetic traffic. First up is the request list: all requests streaming in with quick filters for model, route, status code, and latency.

[01:40] [screen share noise]

[01:45] Evan Brooks: I'll filter to errors only. You can see we show aggregated error spikes on the timeline with a heatmap. If you click any spike, it opens the request inspector which correlates the request to its trace id, the model variant, quantization profile, and routing policy.

[02:05] Priya Nair: Are traces sampled? We can't miss the rare failure pattern.

[02:12] Evan Brooks: By default we do adaptive sampling focused on anomalies and errors — but for pilot you can enable full trace capture for a particular project or time window. That will increase storage but gives full per-token timelines.

[02:30] Liam Ortega: How is PII handled in full capture?

[02:34] Evan Brooks: Two layers: on ingest we can apply redaction rules (regex or field-based) and at rest logs are encrypted with customer-managed KMS. We can also hash tokens or store only token metadata. We'll send the exact config options.

[02:52] [crosstalk]

[02:56] Evan Brooks: Here's an example request — status 502. The inspector shows header, payload (redacted in this demo), response, and a small timeline: SDK call -> routing -> model inference -> response. Note the latency jump at model init.

[03:16] Aisha Bello: That model init — is that a cold start? We have pinned models and warm pools for our heavy jobs.

[03:22] Evan Brooks: Exactly — the trace marks cache warmups and KV cache misses. In the timeline you can hover the KV cache row (occasionally shown as K-V cash in some auto transcripts, sorry) and see hit/miss ratios per request.

[03:38] Priya Nair: We've seen K-V mismatch spikes — how fine-grained are those metrics?

[03:44] Evan Brooks: They are per-request-level with per-token counters when you enable token-level telemetry. For production we recommend sampling, but for a targeted investigation you can enable full token-level capture for a short window.

[03:58] Maya Chen: One thing customers like: request playback. Evan, can you show how playback and compare works?

[04:04] Evan Brooks: Sure — I'll click 'playback' which replays the same request against the pinned model version and a fallback variant. We sandbox the run against a read-only copy of the model that's isolated from customer data; outputs are annotated and diffed to highlight divergence and regressed tokens.

[04:22] Liam Ortega: That sounds useful. Does playback incur cost?

[04:27] Evan Brooks: Minimal — we throttle playback runs and they count as diagnostics which are discounted in pilot programs. We'll include the exact pricing in follow-up.

[04:38] [00:04:50] Evan Brooks: Here's an example of a 502 spike — when I open the trace we can see multiple retries from the SDK, and the gateway fallback to a smaller quantized variant. Notice the sequence where token generation stalls at ~t+1.2s leading to a gateway timeout.

[05:04] Priya Nair: So the SDK retries are increasing load and pushing the next instance over memory?

[05:10] Evan Brooks: Possibly. The trace helps you see retry storms; we surface retry counts, backoff intervals, and which component returned the 502 — gateway, model container, or allocator. In this trace the container OOM isn't obvious, but the allocator queue length spikes then you see queue drain errors.

[05:30] Aisha Bello: Can the console correlate infra metrics? Like GPU memory and host-level OOM logs?

[05:36] Evan Brooks: For Dedicated and Private deployments we integrate with Prometheus/CloudWatch metrics and will surface GPU memory, host OOM events, and pod-level logs inline. For hosted customers we provide aggregated allocator metrics and stack-level indicators.

[05:52] [06:00] Priya Nair: What about alerts and automated runbooks? We want to avoid paging our SREs for a transient glitch.

[06:07] Evan Brooks: You can configure alert thresholds on error rate, tail latency, or resource signals and attach automatic playbooks — e.g., scale out, trigger cache flush, or fallback to a cheaper variant. We can also trigger a canary routing policy automatically.

[06:24] Liam Ortega: Is there RBAC around who can see full payloads? We need separation for e.g., CS can't see PII.

[06:30] Evan Brooks: Yes — role-based access to logs and playback. You can restrict 'view payload' and 'run playback' to specific roles. We also have SSO/SAML integration and audit trails for every action.

[06:44] [06:50] Priya Nair: Nice. Could you show a real investigation flow end-to-end?

[06:52] Evan Brooks: Sure — open an error window — this one at 02:13 UTC shows a cluster of 5xx. Click on the aggregated group, then drill into a representative request. I open request inspector, then open trace, then hit 'open playback.' The trace shows three retry attempts — attempt 1 succeeds but with 800ms, attempt 2 times out, attempt 3 retries. The gateway then returns a 502 back to the client.

[07:22] Evan Brooks: I then click 'correlate' which finds other requests with the same user session, and 'group by model version' which surfaces that the bad requests all hit a specific quantized variant we recently put behind a routing policy for cost savings.

[07:40] Aisha Bello: So that routing policy change probably introduced a lower-memory variant that can't handle certain long-range context?

[07:45] Evan Brooks: That's a common pattern. In the console we show model capability tags and recommended max seq length per variant; if you exceed that you see stalls and model-side failures.

[07:58] Maya Chen: On the commercial side, if you want to avoid that we recommend a canary rollout for variant changes and automatic rollback based on error/regression metrics — Evan can show the rollout UI quickly.

[08:10] Evan Brooks: Rollouts are configured per model route; you can set weights, automatic checks (latency, error, output-quality via eval sets), and an automatic fallback if quality or SLOs degrade.

[08:26] [08:32] Liam Ortega: About the eval sets — we need to run our actual prompts to detect regressions. How do we feed those in?

[08:36] Evan Brooks: You can upload prompt sets into 'Optimize' and bind them to a route. During rollout we run the set at configured intervals to surface quality regressions. We'll walk through onboarding prompt sets in the pilot runbook.

[08:52] Priya Nair: Cool. A couple of security questions: retention defaults, log encryption, and whether we can opt for on-prem deployment where logs never leave our VPC.

[09:04] Evan Brooks: For Private you can opt for on-prem — logs stay in your VPC and we only have the control plane. For hosted we keep logs in encrypted buckets with configurable retention; default is 90 days but we can tighten to 30 and apply redaction rules pre-ingest.

[09:22] [09:30] Aisha Bello: Any gotchas with our current EKS setup? We use Istio and sidecars.

[09:35] Evan Brooks: Most customers with service meshes use our sidecar-compatible SDK or route via the API gateway. We'll provide a network diagram for recommended egress and NAT rules.

[09:50] Maya Chen: Quick qualification: what's your target timeline for a pilot? Priya?

[09:56] Priya Nair: We'd like an initial 4–6 week pilot in January to validate both traces and playback against our heavy grading batches, and to test redaction and SSO. Budget is there but we need the security docs.

[10:10] Evan Brooks: Great — we'll schedule a 2-hour pilot kickoff with Liam and the infra team. Evan will own the runbook.

[10:18] [10:24] Priya Nair: Back to the trace view — I noticed the trace ID has a linkable URL. Can we export a bundle for offline forensic?

[10:30] Evan Brooks: Yes — export as a zip of the trace, request payloads (redacted if requested), and linked infra metrics. That bundle is useful for postmortems and you can upload into your ticketing system.

[10:44] Liam Ortega: If we run the pilot with full trace capture, how much storage are we talking?

[10:49] Evan Brooks: Depends on token volume; we estimate the pilot will add ~20–40GB/day with full token capture for grading windows. We'll provide estimates based on your sample prompts.

[11:05] Aisha Bello: Can you show alert chaining? e.g., error spike -> runbook -> temp rollback?

[11:10] Evan Brooks: Yep — here's an example alert policy that on >2% 5xx for 5 minutes runs the automated job to lower variant weight by 30% and triggers a Slack incident channel.

[11:24] [11:30] Priya Nair: One more question: we have a strict compliance requirement to show who viewed raw payloads; does Redwood log playback runs?

[11:36] Evan Brooks: Every playback and verb showing payload is audited — user, timestamp, and justification. You can pull audit logs for SOC2.

[11:46] Maya Chen: Wrapping up — we showed request inspector, trace correlation, playback, rollouts, and alerting. Any remaining open concerns?

[11:58] Priya Nair: Main open items: redaction proof, pilot runbook, and a pricing quote for the 3-month pilot.

[12:06] Liam Ortega: I'll validate network diagram with Evan.

[12:08] Aisha Bello: I'll share our prompts and sample loads.

[12:12] Maya Chen: Perfect. We'll follow up with the SOC2 pack, pilot runbook, and schedule the kickoff.

[12:20] Evan Brooks: Quick note — I saw one more pattern in the trace where a small subset of requests had very high token churn because the prompt included large student attachments; for those you'll want a larger memory variant or prefix caching. We'll put suggested config in the runbook.

[12:38] Priya Nair: Good catch. That aligns with our grading spike hypothesis.

[12:42] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone. We'll email the next steps and action items.

[12:48] [End of meeting]
